subsection.title: Stopping criteria
subsection.p: A computer almost never lands on the exact root. It produces a sequence
and we must decide when the sequence is good enough.
There are two numbers we can easily monitor.
First, we can monitor the residual:
This tells us how close the function value is to 0.
Second, we can monitor the step size:
This tells us how much the iterates are still moving.
Both are useful. Neither is perfect by itself.

The maximum iteration count is not mathematical decoration. It protects us from cycles, divergence, and programming mistakes.

paragraphs.title: Why residual alone can mislead
paragraphs.p: A small residual does not always mean a small error in x. The reason is slope.
If the graph is very flat near the axis, then the function value can be small even when the input is not very close to the root.
If a careless stopping rule accepts every residual less than 0.02, then x=0 would be accepted even though it is one million units away from the root.
The residual must be interpreted together with the scale of the function and the slope near the root.

p.me: \text{Small \(f(x_n)\) is strongest evidence when \(f'\) is not small near the root.}

paragraphs.title: Why step size alone can mislead
paragraphs.p: A small step size can also be misleading. An iteration may stop moving because of roundoff error, because the derivative is badly scaled, or because the method is trapped near a point that is not a root.
So a step-size test should usually be paired with a residual test. We want the iterates to stop moving and the function value to be close to zero.

exercise.title: Why is neither residual nor step size enough by itself?

statement.p: A Newton iteration can monitor |f(x_n)| and |x_n-x_{n-1}|. In your own words, why can a small residual occur far from a root, and why can a small step occur even when the current point is not a trustworthy root?

hint.p: A flat graph can have a small function value far from the axis. An iteration can also stall from roundoff, a tiny derivative, or a trap that is not a root. Pair the two tests.

note.title: Practical lesson
note.p: When Newton’s method is converging well to a simple root, the number of correct digits often roughly doubles from one step to the next.
When it is not converging well, no stopping rule should pretend that it is.

exercise.title: Why does a multiple root slow Newton’s method?

statement.p: Near a simple root, Newton’s method often doubles the number of correct digits. Near a double root, the error may merely be cut in half each step. In your own words, what geometric difference between a simple crossing and a flat touch explains the change?

hint.p: Quadratic convergence near a simple root uses a nonzero derivative there. At a root of finite multiplicity m>1, ordinary Newton iteration usually has only linear convergence, with leading error factor (m-1)/m. Such a root can touch or cross the axis.

warning.title: Multiple-root warning
warning.p: If Newton’s method converges only linearly, one possible reason is that the root is multiple.
Repeatedly small residuals with slow-moving iterates may indicate a flat crossing or a flat touch near the axis.

subsection.title: A first glimpse of chaotic iteration
subsection.p: Newton’s method is an iteration:
where
So Newton’s method is not only a root-finding formula. It is also a dynamical system: a rule that sends each point to a next point.
Under the local convergence hypotheses, a simple root attracts Newton iterates started sufficiently close to it.
Far from a root, the dynamics can be complicated.

exercise.title: What can Newton’s method do far from a good root?

statement.p: Newton's method can converge rapidly near a simple root yet fail from another starting value. Describe possible failures and explain which quantities should be monitored during iteration.

hint.p: The method can jump to another root, cycle, divide by zero, or behave unpredictably. Record residual and step size, and restart or switch methods if the residual does not drop.

warning.title: Computational warning
warning.p: Newton’s method can be extremely fast near a good root. Far from a good root, it can move to a different root, enter a cycle, become undefined, or behave unpredictably.

subsection.p: Practical use of Newton's method requires checks on convergence, residuals, and the computed iterates.

subsection.title: A safe Newton workflow
subsection.p: When using Newton’s method as a numerical algorithm, follow a disciplined workflow.

li.p: Choose a function f whose root solves the original problem.
Choose a starting value x_0 from a graph, table, physical estimate, or bracket.
At each step, record x_n, f(x_n), and x_n-x_{n-1}.
Stop only when the residual and step size are both small enough.
If the method leaves the physical domain, cycles, or fails to reduce the residual, restart with a better initial guess or use a safer method such as bisection.

subsection.p: Newton’s method is a perfect example of this chapter’s theme. Calculus gives the idea: follow the tangent line. Computation adds the discipline: check whether the idea is working.
The same discipline belongs to numerical integration. We have formulas, but formulas become understanding only when we test them.
